finding: Assertion loosened from the git-failure message to any non-empty reason.
why: `settings == "failed"` can also come from `_restore_repo_settings` or `_remove_backup`, so the test no longer proves the git-unreadable branch ran.
fix: Assert a fragment that only that branch emits, for example `"git cannot read this repository" in answer["reason"]`.

criterion: behaviour-preservation risk (reworked control flow in an existing method)
finding: A raising cleanup step in the failure path replaces the original error, and a raising chmod skips the temp-file drop.
why: The caller catches OSError and reports the message, so the real cause is lost, and each cleanup step can stop the next.
fix: Run each cleanup step under `contextlib.suppress(OSError)` so both run and the original error propagates.

criterion: Erratic test / Obscure Test (the fix is only exercised on one OS)
finding: The new mode-restore test is vacuous on POSIX: it passes with the old and the new statement order.
why: `unlock` is false off Windows, so the restore never runs and the mode assertion holds regardless of order; a Linux CI pass proves nothing about the fix.
fix: Skip the test off Windows so a pass there is not read as coverage.
evidence: places.py `unlock = exists and os.name == "nt"`; the test has no skipif and ends `assert target.stat().st_mode == before`

criterion: Fragile test (the raised error is not identified)
finding: One stub raises the same PermissionError for os.replace and Path.unlink, so the test cannot tell which error reached the caller.
why: A later change to the cleanup error would pass unnoticed.
fix: Use two stubs with distinct messages and assert with `match=` which error propagates.
evidence: `def locked(*_args): raise PermissionError("locked")` bound to both; `with pytest.raises(PermissionError):`
